Summary:
Before the detail, here is where the story ends up.

The integration is healthy: usage is up 13% in a year and the service is reliable. But 42% of the money PartnerBank customers send (£165.7M of £393.6M) goes around the app to Wise directly, and 35% of all money leaves because of limits in today's app.

That shapes the four answers. Fix the limits together (Question 1). Add a fee carefully, with a test (Question 2). Use what customers already do on Wise to back the multi-currency account case (Question 3). And for Wise, judge that product on new revenue only and pilot it first (Question 4).

Now let's start at the beginning, with what is going well.
Momentum:
The story starts with good news. More PartnerBank customers check the Wise fee in the app every month: 11,260 in April 2025, 12,680 by March 2026, up 13%.

And they don't just look. 76% of the people who check the fee go on to send money. That is a strong sign the price and the speed feel right.

So customers like the product. The next question is whether the service holds up when they use it.
Service quality:
It does. 96.6% of transfers started in the app go through, 77% arrive in under 20 seconds, and the fee appears in 179 milliseconds.

This matters for the rest of the story. Customers are not leaving because the service is slow or unreliable. So if money is going somewhere else, the reason must be something the app doesn't offer yet. That is the twist on the next slide.
The opportunity:
Here is the twist. Over the same year, PartnerBank customers sent £227.9M through the bank's app and another £165.7M through Wise directly, paid straight from their PartnerBank accounts. That is 42% of everything they sent going around the app.

And that group is growing faster: customers using Wise directly grew 31%, 2.4 times as fast as the app.

The bank keeps the customer but loses the transaction. The good news is these are the bank's own customers, already sending this money, so it is the easiest growth there is. But first we need to know why they go around the app.
Why it leaves:
The data answers that. Every Wise-direct transfer was given one reason it couldn't go through the app, and four limits explain 35% of all the money, £138.6M a year.

The biggest by money is the £50,000 limit (£58.7M), but that is only about 940 customers making very large transfers. The one that touches the most people is missing currencies (£37.8M, about 11,600 customers). Then come transfers sent from euros or dollars (£22.1M) and business customers the app can't serve (£20.0M).

Two grey rows are a different story: £14.8M could already have gone through the app, which is about awareness, and £12.3M is accounts and cards, which we come back to in Question 3.

Missing currencies reach the most customers, so let's look closer at those.
Currency coverage:
There are 18 currencies the app doesn't offer, and customers sent £37.8M a year to them through Wise instead. But we don't need all 18 to make a difference.

Just three, the Pakistani rupee, the Bangladeshi taka and the Japanese yen, make up 72% of that money. They are also the most populous countries on the brief's list, and Pakistan and Bangladesh have large UK communities who send money home every month, so the demand is steady.

That gives the bank a focused first step. But not every opportunity needs a new feature. Some customers have already said yes and just haven't started.
Activation:
24,720 people signed up through the app this year. Only 12,240 of them, 50%, made a first transfer. That leaves 12,480 people who chose the product and stopped before using it.

Winning them is cheaper than finding new customers. Every 10-point improvement adds about 2,472 new senders a year. Simple things can help: show the fee and arrival time up front, let people save a recipient during sign-up, and send a reminder a few days later.

Now we have the whole picture, so let's turn it into a plan.
What we recommend:
Putting it together: if we win back half of the money the app could realistically keep, that is about £76.7M more through PartnerBank's app every year.

The plan has four steps. First, add the missing currencies, starting with those three. It reaches the most customers. Second, review the £50,000 limit. It is the most money, from a small group of high-value customers, and it will need risk and compliance input. Third, let customers send from the euros and dollars they already hold. Fourth, fix the first-transfer journey for the 12,480 people waiting.

We agree to track one number together every quarter: the share of customers' money that goes through the app.

Of course, keeping more money in the app only helps the bank if it earns something on it. That is exactly what PartnerBank asked about next: a convenience fee.
Fee design:
Start with the design: 0.3% of each transfer, never less than £1 and never more than £15.

A percentage is fair because it grows with the amount. The minimum covers the cost of tiny transfers, and the cap protects big ones, so someone sending £10,000 pays £15, not £30.

It also stays competitive. HSBC charges £5 and Lloyds £9.50 on many international payments, so PartnerBank's fee is lower than HSBC's below £1,667 and lower than Lloyds' below £3,167. The typical app transfer is about £1,500.

But a good design on paper doesn't tell us how customers will react. That is the real question.
Effect on usage:
Some customers will send less. Small transfers feel the fee most: £1 is 2% of a £50 transfer. The good news is that only 3% of app transfers are £250 or less, so most people pay well under 1%.

If nobody changed their behaviour, the fee would bring in about £562k a year. But some will stop, and the biggest risk is that they move to Wise directly or another provider. That would make the gap from Question 1 bigger.

We can't know how many will stop by guessing, so we test it. Split customers at random into a fee group and a no-fee group, show the full cost before they confirm, run it for at least two months, and agree in advance when to stop. Then we need to know what to watch.
KPIs:
Fee income alone would make any fee look like a success, so we watch customer behaviour alongside it, always comparing the fee group with the no-fee group.

The first warning sign would be fewer people sending after checking the fee (today 76%), or fewer new customers making a first transfer (today 50%). We also watch how much each customer sends, how many move to Wise directly, and complaints.

The decision comes down to one number: extra revenue per customer, counting the customers who stopped. If it is positive and the warning signs stay calm, the fee stays.

That covers sending money. Next, PartnerBank asked about a new product.
Evidence:
Here is what they already do. Of the 25,240 PartnerBank customers who used Wise directly, 4,220, or 17%, already hold a Wise multi-currency account. 7,640 use an account, a card or receive money on Wise.

That is stronger than any survey, because it is real behaviour. These customers already hold foreign currency, just outside their bank. Wise could also share how often they use it and which currencies they hold, to show the bank what it is missing.

One honest caveat: these customers already chose Wise, so they are keener than the average PartnerBank customer. They are perfect for designing and testing a pilot, but not for forecasting the whole bank.

Which leads to the last question: if Wise built this as a platform product, should it invest?
Wise internal:
The key idea is new revenue. Some of these customers already earn Wise money through Wise directly. If a bank account just moves that revenue around, Wise hasn't gained anything. An account earns about £2.50 a month, but £0.50 of that is revenue Wise already gets from these customers. So only £2.00, or 80p in every £1, is genuinely new.

Then I take off the costs: £300k to build, £20k to launch each partner, and the cost of running and activating accounts.

In the base case (3 partners, 5% of customers opening an account) Wise earns £724k of new revenue in three years, but still hasn't paid back the investment. It only pays back, in month 22, if adoption and revenue beat the base case. In the downside, it ends £415k short.

So the whole case rests on two unknowns. That points to the answer.
Wise internal 2:
The answer is not yes or no. It is: learn first.

Revenue is the north star, but it isn't the only test. We also weigh the cost and payback, the engineering time and what it delays, the safeguarding and licensing work that holding balances brings, how strong the evidence really is, and what else that team could build. For example, the Send Money limits from Question 1 already have £138.6M of money behind them.

So the recommendation is to fund one partner pilot, with clear targets for adoption, new revenue per account, and reliability and fraud, and decide go or stop after six months.

That brings the story full circle. The partnership is working. The biggest growth is money PartnerBank customers already send. And every next step, from currencies to the fee to a new account, is something we test and prove together.
Appendix:
If anyone asks how the numbers were made: the dataset has 10,000 records covering all 12 data points in the brief, from April 2025 to March 2026. The brief shows about 33,000 customers checking the fee each quarter and the sample had 1,608, so counts and money are multiplied by 20. Percentages and per-transfer rules use the real transfer sizes, so they don't change.

With real data, the first things I would ask for are a link between each fee check and its transfer, sign-up dates, the partner contract, and the reasons customers give for leaving.
